entries.name: Neon
prose: Serverless Postgres that scales to zero.
entries.pick: you need real Postgres with zero cold-start cost, instant branching for preview deployments, and you refuse to babysit connection pools or idle instances.

alternatives.name: Supabase
alternatives.text: Neon is pure database; pick Supabase when you also want auth, storage, and REST auto-generated from your schema. Pick Neon when you want raw Postgres control without BaaS opinions.

alternatives.name: Turso
alternatives.text: Neon gives you full Postgres (joins, extensions, JSONB); Turso gives you SQLite semantics with edge-local reads. Pick Turso for read-heavy global apps; pick Neon for complex relational queries and migrations tooling.

entries.name: Turso
prose: LibSQL at the edge — strong for read-heavy apps.
entries.pick: your app is read-heavy (dashboards, content sites, analytics) and you want embedded replicas that sit next to your compute for sub-millisecond reads without a connection round-trip.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare D1
alternatives.text: Both are SQLite-at-edge. Pick D1 if you're already on Cloudflare Workers and want zero-config binding. Pick Turso if you deploy on Vercel/Fly/Deno and need a portable edge DB with embedded replicas you control.

alternatives.name: Neon
alternatives.text: Pick Turso when reads dominate and you want edge locality. Pick Neon when you need Postgres features (CTEs, full-text search, extensions) or write-heavy transactional workloads.

entries.name: Supabase

fields.Limits: 0.5 GB DB · 50k MAU · pauses after 7d idle

prose: Postgres BaaS with auth, storage, and REST out of the box.
entries.pick: you want a complete backend — auth, file storage, realtime subscriptions, and auto-generated REST/GraphQL — without stitching separate services together, and you still want raw Postgres access when the abstractions aren't enough.

alternatives.name: Appwrite Cloud
alternatives.text: Both are BaaS. Pick Supabase when you want real Postgres underneath (migrations, extensions, SQL). Pick Appwrite when you prefer a self-hostable, vendor-neutral platform with a simpler permissions model.

alternatives.name: Neon
alternatives.text: Pick Supabase when you want the full platform (auth, storage, edge functions) in one dashboard. Pick Neon when you only need the database and want to pair it with your own auth/storage choices.

entries.name: Upstash Redis
prose: Serverless Redis for cache and queues.
entries.pick: you need a fast key-value layer for caching, rate-limiting, session tokens, or lightweight queues — and you want per-request pricing with no always-on instance to manage.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare KV/D1
alternatives.text: Pick Upstash when you need Redis data structures (sorted sets, pub/sub, Lua scripts) or when your stack isn't on Cloudflare. Pick D1/KV when you're already on Workers and want zero-network-hop access.

alternatives.name: a primary database (Neon/Turso)
alternatives.text: Upstash is a complement, not a replacement. Use it as the caching/queue layer in front of your relational store, not as your source of truth.

entries.name: Convex
prose: Reactive backend with realtime sync for collaborative UIs.
entries.pick: you're building a collaborative or realtime-first app (multiplayer editors, live dashboards, chat) in TypeScript and you want the database, server functions, and realtime subscriptions as one coherent system — no SQL, no ORM, no WebSocket plumbing.

alternatives.name: Supabase Realtime
alternatives.text: Supabase bolts realtime onto Postgres via change-data-capture; Convex is reactive from the ground up. Pick Convex when every query must live-update. Pick Supabase when you also need traditional REST endpoints and raw SQL escape hatches.

alternatives.name: Firebase
alternatives.text: Convex gives you TypeScript-native server functions with full ACID transactions; Firebase gives you a proprietary SDK with weaker consistency. Pick Convex for type-safe, transactional realtime; Firebase if you need its massive mobile ecosystem.

entries.name: Cloudflare D1

fields.Limits: 5 GB / DB · 5M rows read/day on free Workers

prose: SQLite at the edge on Workers.
entries.pick: you're already on Cloudflare Workers and want a database that's a first-class binding — zero network hop, zero connection overhead, deployed alongside your code at the edge.

alternatives.name: Turso
alternatives.text: Both are edge SQLite. Pick D1 when your compute is Workers (native binding, no SDK needed). Pick Turso when you deploy elsewhere (Vercel, Fly, Deno) or need embedded replicas inside your app process.

alternatives.name: Neon
alternatives.text: Pick D1 for simple schemas and edge-speed reads on Workers. Pick Neon when you need full Postgres (complex joins, extensions, large write throughput) or when your app lives outside the Cloudflare ecosystem.

entries.name: MongoDB Atlas M0
prose: Classic document store, free forever shared cluster.
entries.pick: your data is naturally document-shaped (nested objects, variable fields per record), you want a flexible schema that evolves without migrations, and you value the massive MongoDB ecosystem (Mongoose, Atlas Search, Charts).

alternatives.name: Neon/Supabase
alternatives.text: Pick MongoDB when your data doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns (CMS entries, event logs, IoT payloads). Pick Postgres (Neon/Supabase) when you need relational integrity, joins, and strong typing.

alternatives.name: Convex
alternatives.text: Both handle schema-flexible data. Pick Convex for realtime-first TypeScript apps. Pick MongoDB when you want a mature query language (aggregation pipeline), driver support in every language, and a proven path to massive scale.

entries.name: Appwrite Cloud
prose: Auth + DB + Functions in one BaaS.
entries.pick: you want a Firebase-like all-in-one platform (auth, database, functions, storage) that's fully open-source and self-hostable — giving you an exit door that proprietary BaaS platforms don't offer.

alternatives.name: Supabase
alternatives.text: Both are open-source BaaS. Pick Supabase when you want real Postgres and SQL power. Pick Appwrite when you prefer a document-style API, simpler permission rules, and don't need raw SQL.

alternatives.name: PocketBase
alternatives.text: Both are self-hostable. Pick PocketBase for a single-binary zero-dependency deploy on one VPS. Pick Appwrite when you need managed cloud hosting, multiple runtimes for functions, and a larger team/community behind the platform.

entries.name: PocketBase
prose: Single-binary BaaS — SQLite, auth, files, realtime without a cloud bill.
entries.pick: you want the simplest possible self-hosted backend — one binary, no Docker required, zero monthly cost on a free-tier VPS — and your app is small-to-medium scale where SQLite's single-writer model is fine.

alternatives.name: Supabase
alternatives.text: Pick PocketBase when you want total ownership with no cloud dependency and your traffic fits one machine. Pick Supabase when you need horizontal scale, managed infra, and Postgres features.

alternatives.name: Appwrite
alternatives.text: Both are open-source BaaS. Pick PocketBase for radical simplicity (single Go binary, embed in your app). Pick Appwrite for a richer feature set (multiple function runtimes, team collaboration, managed cloud option).

entries.name: Cloudflare Workers & Pages
prose: Edge functions + unlimited static hosting.
entries.pick: your app is a static frontend + API routes and you want zero cold starts at the edge with the most generous free static tier available — no bandwidth caps, no sleep, no containers to manage.

alternatives.name: Vercel Hobby:
alternatives.text: Both deploy static + functions, but Workers runs on 300+ edge locations with no commercial-use restriction; Vercel locks you to hobby/non-commercial on the free plan. **vs Render:** Render gives you a container that sleeps after 15 min; Workers never sleeps and responds in <50 ms globally.

entries.name: Koyeb
prose: Managed containers that stay up 24/7 on free micro.
entries.pick: you need a container that never sleeps — Discord bots, background workers, or long-running processes that must stay warm without paying. Koyeb's free micro runs 24/7 with zero cold-start penalty.

alternatives.name: Render:
alternatives.text: Render's free web services sleep after 15 min of inactivity (30–60 s cold starts); Koyeb stays awake permanently. **vs Railway:** Railway gives ~$5/mo in credits that run out; Koyeb's free instance is truly unlimited hours.

entries.name: Vercel Hobby
prose: Next.js-native deploys. Personal projects only.
entries.pick: you're building a Next.js side project and want the tightest integration possible — ISR, middleware, image optimization, and preview deployments all work out of the box with zero config. Accept the non-commercial restriction and enjoy the DX.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Pages:
alternatives.text: Cloudflare allows commercial use and has no bandwidth cap, but Next.js support is partial (no streaming RSC, limited middleware); Vercel is the canonical Next.js host. **vs Netlify:** Netlify also deploys Next.js but lags behind on latest features and has tighter build-minute limits.

entries.name: Railway
prose: Git-push containers with a small monthly credit.
entries.pick: you want the simplest git-push-to-deploy container experience with databases, cron, and private networking included — and you're okay spending $5/mo once the free credit runs out. Railway treats containers as first-class: Postgres, Redis, and workers all live in one project.

alternatives.name: Render:
alternatives.text: Render's free tier sleeps and the free Postgres expires after 30 days; Railway's $5 credit covers always-on compute + persistent DB. **vs Koyeb:** Koyeb gives you one always-free micro, but Railway gives a full project graph (app + DB + worker) under one credit pool.

entries.name: Render

fields.Limits: 750 hrs/mo · sleep after 15m · free Postgres expires 30d

prose: Web services without a credit card. Sleeps when idle.
entries.pick: you want to ship a demo or portfolio app with zero financial commitment — no credit card, no trial expiry, no surprise bills. The 15-minute sleep is fine for anything that tolerates a cold start on first hit (portfolio sites, demo APIs, interview take-homes).

alternatives.name: Koyeb:
alternatives.text: Koyeb never sleeps but limits you to one 512 MB micro; Render gives 750 free hours across multiple services (useful for multi-service demos). **vs Railway:** Railway requires a credit card and charges after credits are gone; Render stays free forever if you accept the sleep trade-off.

matrixCells.limits: 750 hrs/mo · sleep after 15m · free Postgres expires 30d

entries.name: Netlify
prose: JAMstack hosting + serverless functions.
entries.pick: you're shipping a static site or SPA that needs a few serverless functions for forms, auth, or API proxying — and you want 100 GB bandwidth free without worrying about cold containers or edge-runtime constraints. Netlify's build plugins and form handling are unmatched for content sites.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Pages:
alternatives.text: Cloudflare has no bandwidth cap and faster edge functions, but Netlify's build plugin ecosystem (CMS previews, form handling, split testing) is richer for content-heavy JAMstack. **vs Vercel Hobby:** Netlify allows commercial use on the free tier; Vercel Hobby restricts you to non-commercial projects.

entries.name: Deno Deploy
prose: TypeScript at the edge; pairs with Deno KV.
entries.pick: you're writing TypeScript/Deno-native code and want an edge runtime with built-in KV storage — no external database required for small apps. 1M requests/month free makes it viable for real production traffic, not just demos.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Workers:
alternatives.text: Both are edge runtimes, but Deno Deploy uses standard Web APIs + Deno KV with zero config; Workers requires learning KV/D1 bindings and the Cloudflare-specific module system. **vs Vercel Edge Functions:** Vercel's edge runtime is a thin layer on top of their Node platform; Deno Deploy is the runtime itself with first-party KV, giving you a complete backend in one place.

entries.name: Oracle Cloud Always Free

fields.Limits: 2× AMD VMs + 4 ARM OCPUs · 200 GB block

prose: Real VMs forever — if you survive signup.
entries.pick: you need actual Linux VMs with root access, persistent storage, and serious compute (4 ARM OCPUs + 24 GB RAM is more than most $50/mo VPS plans) — and you're patient enough to fight Oracle's signup lottery. Once provisioned, these run any stack: Docker, K3s, databases, game servers, whatever.

alternatives.name: Koyeb/Render/Railway:
alternatives.text: Those are managed PaaS with opinionated runtimes; Oracle gives you bare metal control — install anything, run anything, no platform lock-in. **vs Fly.io:** Fly gives you global distribution but charges per GB/hour; Oracle gives you one region but 24 GB RAM free forever.

matrixCells.limits: 2× AMD VMs + 4 ARM OCPUs · 200 GB block

entries.name: Coolify

fields.Limits: OSS · unlimited apps on your infra

prose: Self-hosted PaaS — Heroku/Render shape on your VPS.
entries.pick: you already have a VPS (Oracle Always Free, Hetzner, etc.) and want a Heroku-like UI for deploying unlimited apps without per-service fees. Coolify handles git deploys, SSL, databases, and backups — you own the entire stack.

alternatives.name: Railway/Render:
alternatives.text: Those charge per service or impose free-tier limits; Coolify is free and unlimited — you only pay for the underlying VM. **vs Oracle Cloud alone:** Oracle gives you the VM but no deployment tooling; Coolify turns that raw VM into a one-click PaaS with auto-SSL and Docker Compose support.

entries.name: Clerk
prose: Pre-built auth UI for B2B/B2C.
entries.pick: you want auth working in an afternoon, not a weekend — drop-in `<SignIn/>` components, hosted account portal, and you never write a password-reset flow again. 50 k monthly active users before you pay a cent means most indie projects never outgrow free.

alternatives.name: Kinde:
alternatives.text: Clerk's UI components are richer out-of-the-box (pre-styled modals, user profile pages); Kinde bundles feature flags and SSO at the same tier so you install fewer vendors. Pick Clerk for speed-to-ship; pick Kinde if you also need flags/SSO without another tool.

alternatives.name: Zitadel:
alternatives.text: Clerk is a managed-only service — zero ops, but you can't self-host. Zitadel gives you an OSS escape hatch and 25 k MAU free, but you build your own login UI.

entries.name: Kinde
prose: Auth with SSO and feature flags.
entries.pick: you need auth, enterprise SSO, and feature flags from one vendor so you're not duct-taping Clerk + LaunchDarkly together. Kinde's free tier (~10.5 k MAU) is lower than Clerk's, but the bundled flags and RBAC make it the better consolidated choice for B2B SaaS that will need "is this feature enabled for org X?" logic from day one.

alternatives.name: Clerk:
alternatives.text: Kinde trades Clerk's polished UI kit for built-in feature flags, roles, and SSO — fewer vendors, but you'll style your own login screens. Pick Kinde when your app needs gating and org-level access control early; pick Clerk when pixel-perfect auth UX matters more than bundled infra.

entries.name: Doppler

fields.Limits: 5 users free · Team free via GitHub Pack while student

prose: Secrets sync to Vercel, Koyeb, Railway.
entries.pick: your stack spans multiple deploy targets (Vercel preview + Railway prod + local dev) and you're tired of copy-pasting `.env` values between dashboards. Doppler becomes the single source of truth for secrets and syncs them to each target automatically — one `doppler run` replaces a pile of `.env` files.

alternatives.name: Infisical:
alternatives.text: Doppler is polished SaaS with first-class integrations for Vercel/Railway/Fly; Infisical is open-source and self-hostable. Pick Doppler for zero-ops secret sync across commercial PaaS; pick Infisical if you want an auditable OSS layer you control or need to avoid vendor lock-in on secrets.

matrixCells.limits: 5 users free · Team free via GitHub Pack while student

entries.name: Hookdeck
prose: Webhook ingest with retries and queues.
entries.pick: you receive webhooks from Stripe/Clerk/GitHub and need guaranteed delivery without writing your own retry queue. Hookdeck sits in front of your endpoint, buffers events, retries failures with backoff, and gives you a replay UI — 100 k events/mo free is plenty for indie SaaS webhook traffic.

alternatives.name: rolling your own:
alternatives.text: A custom Bull/Redis queue gives you full control but costs a VPS and maintenance. Hookdeck is zero-infra: point the provider's webhook URL at Hookdeck, point Hookdeck at your app, and get retries + observability for free. Pick Hookdeck until your event volume or latency needs outgrow the managed tier.

entries.name: Infisical

fields.Limits: Free cloud tier for secrets sync

prose: Open-source Doppler alternative.
entries.pick: you want secret management you can audit, fork, and self-host — no vendor can pull the rug on your secrets infra. Infisical's cloud free tier works like Doppler (env sync, integrations), but you also get the option to run it on your own box for compliance or air-gapped setups.

alternatives.name: Doppler:
alternatives.text: Infisical is OSS-first — you can self-host, audit the code, and avoid proprietary lock-in. Doppler has slicker PaaS integrations (one-click Vercel sync) and a more polished CLI UX. Pick Infisical when sovereignty and self-host matter; pick Doppler when you just want secrets to flow to managed platforms with zero ops.

matrixCells.limits: Free cloud tier for secrets sync

entries.name: Zitadel

fields.Limits: ~25k MAU free cloud · OSS self-host unlimited

prose: Cloud-native IdP with passkeys and multi-tenancy — Clerk alternative.
entries.pick: you want a full identity provider (OIDC/SAML/passkeys) you can self-host long-term without per-MAU pricing cliffs. Zitadel's free cloud gives you 25 k MAU to validate, and the OSS binary means you can move to your own infra when margins matter — no rewrite, same API.

alternatives.name: Clerk:
alternatives.text: Zitadel is an IdP you own; Clerk is a widget you rent. Clerk ships faster (drag-and-drop UI), but Zitadel gives you protocol-level control (custom OIDC scopes, SAML federation, machine-to-machine tokens) and no hard vendor ceiling. Pick Zitadel for multi-tenant B2B that will eventually need self-hosted auth; pick Clerk if you want login done in a day and won't self-host.

entries.name: Resend
prose: Transactional email with React Email DX.
entries.pick: your app sends password resets, receipts, or magic links and you want to compose them in JSX/TSX like a React component — not raw HTML tables from 2004. The 3k/mo free tier covers early-stage SaaS without thinking about cost, and the single-domain cap only hurts if you run multiple brands.

alternatives.name: Brevo
alternatives.text: Resend is pure transactional with a modern SDK; Brevo bundles marketing lists and campaigns you won't use yet. **vs SendGrid** — Resend's deliverability is comparable but the DX (React Email templates, instant logs) is a generation ahead of SendGrid's legacy dashboard.

entries.name: Brevo
prose: Marketing + transactional in one forever-free tier.
entries.pick: you need both drip campaigns (welcome sequences, newsletters) and transactional sends (order confirmations) from one platform without stitching two services together. The 300 emails/day forever-free tier is generous enough for a side-project that also wants to nurture a small subscriber list.

alternatives.name: Resend
alternatives.text: Brevo adds a full marketing automation UI; Resend is code-only transactional. **vs Loops** — Brevo is broader (CRM, SMS, chat) but less opinionated about SaaS lifecycle; Loops is purpose-built for product-led onboarding flows.

entries.name: Loops
prose: Product/lifecycle email for SaaS onboarding.
entries.pick: you're building a SaaS and your emails are event-driven: "user signed up → send welcome", "trial day 3 → nudge to activate", "plan cancelled → win-back". Loops is designed around product events, not marketing blasts — the 1k contacts free tier fits pre-PMF perfectly.

alternatives.name: Brevo
alternatives.text: Loops speaks product events natively (user.signed_up, subscription.cancelled); Brevo forces you to map those into generic automation triggers. **vs Resend** — Resend is a pipe (send this template now); Loops owns the timing, segmentation, and sequence logic so you don't build it yourself.

entries.name: Tally / Formspark
prose: Drop-in forms without standing up a backend.
entries.pick: you need a contact form, waitlist signup, or feedback widget on a static site or landing page and refuse to spin up an API just to receive a POST. Tally gives you a Notion-like form builder with unlimited submissions on free; Formspark is a minimal `<form action>` endpoint if you want full HTML control.

alternatives.name: Formspree
alternatives.text: Tally's free tier is far more generous (unlimited submissions vs 50/mo) and the builder is nicer; Formspree wins only if you need its plugin ecosystem or paid validations. **vs building your own** — a serverless function + DB costs $0 too, but takes an afternoon you could spend on your actual product.

entries.name: Twilio Trial

fields.Limits: Trial credit · numbers can be restricted · PAYG after

prose: SMS/voice for OTP and alerts — trial credit, then meter hard.
entries.pick: you need phone-number verification or SMS OTP codes and want the widest global carrier coverage with battle-tested docs. Twilio's trial credit lets you prototype the full flow for free; just know that after the credit burns you're paying per-message with no free floor.

alternatives.name: Vonage
alternatives.text: Twilio has superior documentation, broader SDK support, and more phone-number inventory in most countries. Choose Vonage only when Twilio can't provision a number in your target region or its per-message rate is notably worse there. **vs email OTP** — SMS adds real friction and cost; only use it when regulatory or UX requirements demand phone verification.

matrixCells.limits: Trial credit · numbers can be restricted · PAYG after

entries.name: Vonage (Nexmo)
prose: SMS/voice alternative when Twilio pricing or coverage is awkward.
entries.pick: Twilio can't provision a local number in your target country, charges an unreasonable premium on a specific route, or you want a second vendor for failover. Vonage's API surface is comparable but the signup credit is stingy — treat it as a backup, not a default.

alternatives.name: Twilio
alternatives.text: Vonage occasionally wins on per-SMS pricing in APAC/EMEA corridors and has better WhatsApp Business API coverage in some regions; Twilio wins everywhere else on DX, docs, and ecosystem. **vs email-based OTP** — same trade-off as Twilio: only reach for SMS when a phone number is the trust anchor your product needs.

entries.name: Postmark
prose: Transactional email with serious deliverability — trial then paid.
entries.pick: inbox placement is non-negotiable — invoices, security alerts, or anything where "check your spam folder" is unacceptable. Postmark's entire business model is deliverability-first (they reject bulk marketing senders). The catch: there's no forever-free tier, so use it once your product earns revenue or when you graduate from Resend/SendGrid's free caps.

alternatives.name: Resend
alternatives.text: Postmark has years of deliverability reputation data and dedicated IPs at lower volumes; Resend is newer but the free tier and DX are better for pre-revenue. **vs SendGrid** — Postmark's sending reputation is pristine because they refuse marketing mail; SendGrid's shared IPs are diluted by everyone else's newsletters.

entries.name: Twilio SendGrid

fields.Limits: Free forever ~100 emails/day class · verify current Free plan

prose: Legacy free forever email tier — still useful, watch reputation limits.
entries.pick: you want a permanent free floor (~100 emails/day) for transactional sends and don't mind an older dashboard. SendGrid's free plan has survived multiple Twilio policy changes — verify it still exists before onboarding — but it works if you just need password resets and don't want to think about billing.

alternatives.name: Resend
alternatives.text: SendGrid has more email volume on free (100/day vs Resend's 100/day but 3k/mo cap), but Resend's developer experience, logging, and template tooling are dramatically better. **vs Postmark** — SendGrid is free; Postmark is paid. If you don't yet have revenue and can tolerate shared-IP reputation risk, SendGrid costs nothing.

matrixCells.limits: Free forever ~100 emails/day class · verify current Free plan

entries.name: Formspree
prose: Form backend for static sites — email on submit without a server.
entries.pick: you want a zero-JS form endpoint you can drop into any HTML page with a simple `action=` URL — no build step, no SDK, no client-side code required. The 50 submissions/mo free cap is tight, so this fits low-traffic pages like a portfolio contact form or an internal feedback widget.

alternatives.name: Tally
alternatives.text: Formspree is a raw HTTP endpoint (you own the HTML); Tally is a hosted form builder (you embed their UI). Pick Formspree when you want pixel-perfect form styling. **vs Formspark** — nearly identical concept; Formspree has a slightly richer plugin/integration layer, Formspark is simpler and cheaper at paid tiers.

entries.name: Forward Email

fields.Limits: Unlimited aliases free class · paid for outbound SMTP

prose: Privacy-first custom-domain email forwarding — free MX without a mailbox bill.
entries.pick: you want `hello@yourdomain.com` to land in your personal Gmail/Proton without paying for Google Workspace or a hosted mailbox. Forward Email gives unlimited aliases on the free tier — perfect for receiving support@ or billing@ at your custom domain while keeping a single inbox.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Email Routing
alternatives.text: both are free inbound forwarding; Forward Email is open-source and works with any DNS provider, while Cloudflare Email Routing requires your domain's nameservers on Cloudflare. **vs ImprovMX** — Forward Email's free tier is more generous (unlimited aliases vs 25) and the project is fully open-source with no tracking.

entries.name: Cloudflare R2

fields.Limits: 10 GB · 1M Class A · 10M Class B · $0 egress

prose: S3-compatible object storage with zero egress fees.
entries.pick: you need general-purpose object storage and refuse to pay egress taxes — especially if you're already on Cloudflare Workers or Pages. The 10 GB free tier plus zero egress makes it the default choice for any project that serves files to users.

alternatives.name: Backblaze B2:
alternatives.text: R2 gives you zero egress natively; B2 only waives egress if you route through Cloudflare CDN. R2 also has tighter Workers integration (bindings, no auth overhead). Pick B2 only for cold archive you rarely read.

alternatives.name: Tigris:
alternatives.text: Both are S3-compatible, but R2 is battle-tested at Cloudflare scale with richer ecosystem tooling. Tigris wins if your compute lives on Fly and you want automatic edge replication without CDN config.

matrixCells.limits: 10 GB · 1M Class A · 10M Class B · $0 egress

entries.name: Backblaze B2
prose: Cheap archive storage; egress waived via Cloudflare.
entries.pick: you have cold data (backups, exports, user archives) that's written once and rarely read — and you want the absolute cheapest $/GB at rest. Pair it with a Cloudflare CDN zone to get free egress via the Bandwidth Alliance.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare R2:
alternatives.text: B2 is cheaper per GB stored ($0.005 vs $0.015), but R2's zero egress is unconditional and doesn't require CDN fronting. If you read files frequently, R2 wins on total cost. B2 is the budget cold-storage play.

alternatives.name: Tigris:
alternatives.text: B2 has no edge replication or smart caching — it's a single-region bucket. Tigris is better if latency matters; B2 is better if you just want a cheap vault.

entries.name: UploadThing
prose: File uploads wired for Next.js in minutes.
entries.pick: you're building a Next.js app and want file uploads working in under 30 minutes with zero infra config — presigned URLs, progress callbacks, type-safe routes, and a dashboard included. The 2 GB free tier is tight but perfect for MVPs and prototypes.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare R2:
alternatives.text: R2 gives you raw S3 buckets — you'll wire presigned URLs and client uploaders yourself. UploadThing is a managed upload layer with built-in UI components and callbacks. Pick R2 when you outgrow 2 GB or need full control; pick UploadThing when speed-to-ship matters more.

alternatives.name: Cloudinary:
alternatives.text: Cloudinary transforms media after upload; UploadThing just stores and serves files. If you need resizing, cropping, or format conversion, Cloudinary is the tool. If you just need "user uploads a file, app stores it," UploadThing is simpler.

entries.name: Cloudinary
prose: On-the-fly image and video transforms.
entries.pick: your app is image-heavy or video-heavy and you need resize, crop, format conversion, watermarking, or adaptive streaming without running your own pipeline. The URL-based transform API means zero server code for media manipulation. 25 credits/mo covers a surprising number of transformations for a small SaaS.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare R2:

entries.pick: you need one API key to access OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, and dozens of open models — swap providers without changing code and use free-tier models for dev. **vs Together AI:** OpenRouter aggregates *all* providers (closed + open) behind one endpoint; Together only hosts open-weight models. **vs direct OpenAI/Anthropic:** you trade ~5 % markup for instant fallback routing and cost-ranked model selection.

entries.name: Groq

entries.name: Cloudflare Workers AI

entries.name: Together AI

entries.name: Fireworks AI

entries.name: Anthropic API

entries.name: Replicate

entries.name: Langfuse
prose: LLM observability — traces, costs, evals before your bill surprises you.
entries.pick: you want full-stack LLM observability (traces, token costs, prompt versioning, evals) with an open-source core you can self-host when data residency matters. **vs Helicone:** Langfuse gives you deeper eval/dataset tooling and self-host option; Helicone is simpler to adopt (one URL swap) but cloud-only and shallower on evals. **vs LangSmith:** Langfuse is framework-agnostic and open-source; LangSmith is tightly coupled to LangChain and closed-source.

prose: Proxy for LLM APIs — caching + spend visibility with one base URL swap.
entries.pick: you want instant cost visibility and response caching across all your LLM calls by swapping a single base URL — zero SDK changes, works with any OpenAI-compatible provider. **vs Langfuse:** Helicone is faster to set up (proxy approach, no SDK instrumentation) and adds caching out of the box; Langfuse is deeper on evals, datasets, and self-hosting. **vs building your own logging:** Helicone gives you dashboards, alerts, rate limiting, and user tracking for free — shipping that yourself burns a sprint.

entries.name: Mem0
prose: Managed memory layer for agents so you don't reinvent user context stores.
entries.pick: your agent needs persistent per-user memory (preferences, past interactions, facts) without building your own embedding + retrieval pipeline from scratch. **vs pgvector + custom code:** Mem0 handles memory extraction, deduplication, and decay out of the box; rolling your own means writing and maintaining that logic yourself. **vs LangChain memory modules:** Mem0 is a dedicated managed service with a real API and dashboard; LangChain memory is an in-process abstraction you still need to persist somewhere.

entries.name: Browserbase

prose: Hosted browsers for agent scraping/automation without Playwright ops.
entries.pick: your AI agents need to browse, scrape, or interact with real web pages and you don't want to manage Playwright infrastructure, proxy rotation, or headless Chrome scaling yourself. **vs Browserless:** Browserbase is built specifically for AI agent workflows (session replay, stealth mode, built-in proxies); Browserless is a more general headless Chrome API for PDFs and screenshots. **vs self-hosted Playwright:** Browserbase handles anti-bot evasion, IP rotation, and scaling to hundreds of concurrent sessions — things that take weeks to build reliably on your own infra.

entries.name: Exa
prose: Neural web search for RAG/agents when keyword search is too dumb.
entries.pick: you need semantic web search — find pages by *meaning* rather than keyword match — which is ideal for RAG pipelines, research agents, and "find similar" features where traditional search returns irrelevant noise. **vs Tavily:** Exa uses neural embeddings for semantic matching (better for conceptual queries); Tavily is closer to traditional search (better for factual lookups like "current price of X"). **vs building your own scraper + embeddings:** Exa indexes the web for you and returns content — no crawling, no chunking, no vector DB needed for web knowledge.

Mistral also offers its own proprietary models (Large, Medium) not available elsewhere. **vs OpenAI API:** Mistral is significantly cheaper (PAYG from $0.10/MTok vs $2.50+) with competitive quality on many tasks; OpenAI wins on frontier reasoning benchmarks.

prose: Startup cloud credits — apply via accelerator/partner or Activate Founders.

prose: GCP credits for eligible startups — pair with Skills Boost for learning.
entries.pick: you're building on BigQuery, Vertex AI, or Cloud Run and want $2k–$200k in credits without needing an accelerator sponsor. entries.name: Microsoft for Startups
prose: Azure credits + GitHub/OpenAI perks for accepted startups.
entries.pick: your product depends on OpenAI models (GPT-4, embeddings) or your customers live in Microsoft-land (Teams integrations, Entra ID SSO). The bundled GitHub Enterprise + Azure OpenAI access is uniquely valuable for AI-first startups that need production-grade rate limits day one. **vs AWS Activate:** Azure credits are smaller on average but the OpenAI + GitHub bundle is unmatched; AWS wins on raw infra breadth and community tooling. **vs Google for Startups:** pick Azure when you need GPT-family models or .NET hosting; pick GCP when your differentiator is data/ML pipelines on Vertex.

entries.name: Stripe Atlas

fields.Limits: One-time fee · not a free tier

prose: Incorporate + bank + Stripe in one path — not free, but fewer lawyers early.
entries.pick: you're a non-US founder (or just hate paperwork) and want a Delaware C-Corp + bank account + payment processing live in under two weeks without hiring a lawyer. The $500 one-time fee pays for itself in avoided legal hours. **vs Firstbase/Doola:** Atlas is tighter integrated with Stripe payments and has the largest partner-perk network (AWS credits, Notion, etc.); competitors offer more hand-holding on tax filings but cost more annually. **vs DIY (Clerky + Mercury):** DIY is cheaper upfront if you already have a US address and can self-file; Atlas wins on speed and bundled perks when you're moving fast.

matrixCells.limits: One-time fee · not a free tier

entries.name: Clerk (startup path)
prose: Auth that ships — stay on free MAU until you have users worth billing.
entries.pick: you want polished auth UI (sign-in, user profile, org switcher) shipped in hours instead of days, and you're building with Next.js/React. Clerk's component library and webhook system let you skip writing auth plumbing entirely until 50k monthly active users. **vs Auth0/Okta:** Clerk's DX is years ahead for small teams — embeddable components, simpler pricing, no "contact sales" cliff until you're well-funded; Auth0 wins when you need enterprise SAML/SCIM on day one. **vs Supabase Auth / Firebase Auth:** those are cheaper (free) but give you a bare JWT — you still build every UI and session flow yourself; Clerk trades some lock-in for shipping velocity.

entries.name: PostHog
prose: Product analytics without a $enterprise contract — free until you scale events.
entries.pick: you need session replays, feature flags, A/B tests, AND funnels in one tool and refuse to duct-tape Mixpanel + LaunchDarkly + Hotjar together. PostHog's all-in-one surface means one SDK, one billing meter, one data model to reason about. **vs Mixpanel/Amplitude:** PostHog is warehouse-native and self-hostable; Mixpanel has slightly better collaboration UX for non-technical PMs but costs more per event and locks data in their cloud. **vs Plausible/Umami:** PostHog is for *product* analytics (who clicked what, where they churned); Plausible is for *traffic* analytics (pageviews, referrers) — use Plausible for your marketing site, PostHog for your app.

entries.name: Plausible / Umami

fields.Limits: Umami Cloud free tier · Plausible paid (or self-host)

prose: Privacy-first analytics when PostHog is overkill for a brochure site.
entries.pick: you only need pageviews, referrers, and country breakdowns for a marketing site or docs — and you want a <1 KB script that doesn't trigger cookie banners. Perfect when GDPR compliance matters more than funnel analysis. **vs PostHog:** Plausible/Umami show you *traffic*; PostHog shows you *product behavior*. Don't shoehorn PostHog onto a landing page, and don't expect Umami to tell you where users drop off in onboarding. **vs Google Analytics:** GA4 is free but bloated, cookie-dependent, and feeds Google's ad network — Plausible/Umami give you clean numbers without the privacy trade-off or the learning curve of GA4's data model.

matrixCells.limits: Umami Cloud free tier · Plausible paid (or self-host)

entries.name: Cal.com
prose: Scheduling without Calendly tax — self-host or free cloud seats.
entries.pick: you book demos, interviews, or support calls and refuse to pay $12+/seat/mo for what is essentially a calendar link. Cal.com's free tier covers one calendar + one event type per user, and self-hosting removes all limits. **vs Calendly:** Cal.com is open-source with identical core features (round-robin, collective, workflows) — Calendly only wins on polished integrations (Salesforce, HubSpot) that you don't need pre-PMF. **vs SavvyCal:** SavvyCal has prettier recipient-side UX but no free tier and no self-host option; pick it only if scheduling UX is your competitive moat (it isn't).

entries.name: Crisp / Chatwoot
prose: Customer chat on a budget — Chatwoot self-host if you want $0.
entries.pick: users expect a chat widget in your app and you want to respond from one inbox (not scattered Slack DMs). Chatwoot self-hosted is truly $0 with unlimited agents; Crisp's free tier works if you have ≤2 agents and don't want to run infra. **vs Intercom:** Intercom is 10x the price and 10x the feature bloat — you don't need AI bots, product tours, and a CDP when you have 50 users; Chatwoot/Crisp cover live chat + email inbox which is all that matters pre-scale. **vs Freshdesk:** Freshdesk is ticket-first (email/forms); Crisp/Chatwoot are chat-first (widget). Pick based on whether your users expect real-time replies or async tickets.

entries.name: Linear

fields.Limits: Free for small teams · startup programs exist

prose: Issue tracking that teams actually use — free for small startups.
entries.pick: your team has 2–10 engineers and you want issue tracking that's fast enough that people actually update tickets instead of ignoring them. Linear's keyboard-first UX and opinionated workflows (cycles, triage) reduce process overhead to near zero. **vs Jira:** Jira is where velocity goes to die — it's configurable to the point of paralysis and optimized for enterprise reporting, not shipping. Linear is the anti-Jira. **vs GitHub Issues/Projects:** fine for OSS or solo devs, but GitHub Projects lacks cycles, priorities, triage queues, and the speed that makes Linear sticky for teams. Graduate to Linear once you have >1 person.

matrixCells.limits: Free for small teams · startup programs exist

entries.name: Notion (team)

fields.Limits: Free plan solid · student Plus via Edu

prose: Docs + wiki — Free/Plus until you need SAML; don't buy Enterprise early.
entries.pick: you need one place for specs, meeting notes, onboarding docs, and lightweight project tracking — and your team already thinks in Notion. The free plan is generous for small teams; students get Plus via .edu email. **vs Confluence:** Confluence is Jira's sidekick — if you're not on Atlassian, there's zero reason to use it. Notion is faster to write in, prettier to read, and doesn't require an admin cert to configure. **vs Slite/Coda:** Slite is simpler but less powerful; Coda is more powerful but harder to learn. Notion sits in the sweet spot for 90% of startup wiki needs. Don't overthink this one.

matrixCells.limits: Free plan solid · student Plus via Edu

entries.name: Loom / Screen Studio lite paths

fields.Limits: Loom free caps · or OBS + R2 for $0 hosting

prose: Async demos for sales and support without a video team.
entries.pick: you close deals or resolve support tickets faster with a 2-minute screen recording than a 30-minute call. Loom's free tier (25 videos, 5 min each) covers early sales; for polished product demos, Screen Studio (macOS, one-time $89) gives you Apple-keynote-quality zoom animations without After Effects. **vs writing a doc:** a 90-second Loom replaces a 500-word email and gets watched 3x more often. Use it for anything where "let me show you" beats "let me explain." **vs OBS + R2 self-host:** $0 but no viewer analytics, no comments, no auto-transcripts. Fine for internal walkthroughs; use Loom when you need to know if the prospect actually watched.

matrixCells.limits: Loom free caps · or OBS + R2 for $0 hosting

entries.name: Paddle / Lemon Squeezy

fields.Limits: Fee % of revenue · no monthly until you sell

prose: Merchant of record — taxes/VAT handled so you can sell globally early.
entries.pick: you sell to consumers or small businesses worldwide and refuse to register for VAT in 30 countries. A merchant of record (MoR) is the legal seller — they handle sales tax, VAT, invoicing, and refunds. You get a net payout. Worth the 5% fee to avoid tax compliance nightmares on day one. **vs Stripe direct:** Stripe is a payment processor, not a MoR — *you* are still liable for tax collection and remittance. Use Stripe when you only sell B2B in one country or have a tax tool (Avalara) already. **vs Paddle vs Lemon Squeezy:** Paddle is more mature (subscription dunning, retention tools); Lemon Squeezy is simpler and better for digital products / info products. Pick Lemon Squeezy for solo-founder simplicity, Paddle for SaaS with seat-based billing.

matrixCells.limits: Fee % of revenue · no monthly until you sell

entries.name: Plain / Freshdesk Lite

fields.Limits: Free tiers / trials · graduate when ticket volume hurts

prose: Support inbox when Discord DMs stop scaling.
entries.pick: you've outgrown "check Discord/email manually" and need a shared inbox with assignment, status tracking, and SLA timers — but you're not ready to pay Intercom prices. Plain is developer-first (API-native, thread-based); Freshdesk Lite is more traditional (ticket queue, canned responses, knowledge base). **vs Intercom:** Plain/Freshdesk cost $0–$15/agent vs Intercom's $39+/seat — and you don't need chatbots, product tours, or a CDP at this stage. **vs Crisp/Chatwoot:** those are chat-widget-first; Plain/Freshdesk are inbox/ticket-first. Pick based on your support model: real-time widget conversations → Crisp; async email/form tickets → Plain or Freshdesk.

matrixCells.limits: Free tiers / trials · graduate when ticket volume hurts

entries.name: Fly.io

fields.Limits: No classic free tier for new accounts · small bills if sized right

prose: Global VMs near users — PAYG after free allowances changed; still lean vs hyperscale.
entries.pick: you need your backend within 50ms of users in multiple regions and don't want to learn Terraform + VPCs to get there. Fly gives you Firecracker VMs with a `fly deploy` and handles Anycast, TLS, and private networking. Best for latency-sensitive APIs, real-time apps, or SQLite-on-the-edge patterns. **vs Railway/Render:** Railway and Render are simpler (git-push deploy) but single-region by default; Fly wins when multi-region latency matters. **vs AWS/GCP:** hyperscalers give you infinite knobs but cost $0 in brainpower only if you already know them; Fly trades some flexibility for "deploy globally in 5 minutes" simplicity at <$10/mo for small apps.

matrixCells.limits: No classic free tier for new accounts · small bills if sized right

entries.name: HTMX + Go/Python SSR
prose: Skip SPA tax until product-market fit — fewer JS bundles, cheaper hosting.
entries.pick: your app is CRUD-heavy (dashboards, admin panels, internal tools) and you'd rather ship features than fight React hydration, bundle splitting, and state management. HTMX gives you dynamic UI with server-rendered HTML — no build step, no node_modules, no client-side router. Pair with Go (fast, single binary) or Python/Django (fast iteration, batteries included). **vs Next.js/React SPA:** SPAs win when you need rich offline interactions, real-time collaborative editing, or complex client state (Figma, Notion). For 80% of B2B SaaS, HTMX + SSR is faster to build, faster to load, and cheaper to host. **vs Laravel/Rails:** same philosophy (server-rendered, productive) — pick Go/Python HTMX if you want lighter deployments (single binary or container) without a full framework's opinions.

entries.name: Intercom

fields.Limits: Limited free/trial · expensive at seat scale · anti-reco for day-0

prose: Support suite — free crumbs exist; paywall hits fast. Prefer Chatwoot early.
entries.pick: you have PMF, paying customers, and a support team of 3+ — and you need AI bots, product tours, in-app messaging, and a help center in one integrated platform. Intercom is genuinely good *at scale*; it's just wildly expensive and overpowered for a pre-revenue startup. Do not start here on day zero. **vs Chatwoot/Crisp:** Chatwoot at $0 covers 95% of what you need pre-Series A. Switch to Intercom when you need AI resolution bots, proactive messaging campaigns, or your support volume justifies the $39+/seat/mo cost. **vs Zendesk:** both are enterprise-grade; Intercom is more product-led (in-app messenger), Zendesk is more ticket-led (email/phone). Neither belongs in your stack until you have revenue to burn.

**vs** VS Code + extensions: VS Code is lighter and free forever, but JetBrains wins on deep refactors, integrated profilers, and framework-aware inspections (Spring, Django, .NET). Pick JetBrains when the project is large enough that "go to definition" isn't enough.
entries.pick: you write Java, Kotlin, C#, or Python professionally-sized projects and need refactoring, debugging, and database tooling that actually understands your framework — not just syntax highlighting. The student license gives you _every_ IDE simultaneously, so you never hit a "wrong language" wall.

prose: AI pair programmer free via GitHub Education.

**vs** Codeium / Tabnine free tiers: Copilot has deeper context awareness (whole-repo indexing on Pro) and tighter VS Code/JetBrains integration. Free alternatives are fine for occasional use, but Copilot's multi-file context wins when your project has 50+ files.
entries.pick: you're writing code daily and want inline completions that cut boilerplate in half — especially repetitive tests, data transformations, and API glue. The student tier is the same Pro product; no feature gates.

entries.name: GitHub Codespaces
prose: Cloud dev environments on your personal account.

**vs** Gitpod / local Docker: Gitpod's free tier is stingier on hours and lacks the native GitHub integration (PR codespaces, deep linking). Local Docker is free but requires a capable machine and setup time. Codespaces trades hours-per-month for zero-config parity across devices.
entries.pick: your local machine is underpowered, shared, or locked-down — Codespaces gives you a full Linux dev box in seconds from any browser or thin client. Also ideal when you switch between machines (library desktop → laptop → tablet) and want identical environments without dotfile gymnastics.

entries.name: Azure for Students
prose: $100 credit/year, no credit card, renewable while enrolled.

**vs** AWS Free Tier / GCP Credits: AWS free tier is perpetual but thin (t2.micro only), and requires a credit card. GCP student credits exist but are harder to find and one-shot. Azure renews annually with no card — the safest "learn cloud" sandbox for students who forget to tear down resources.
entries.pick: you need real cloud VMs, databases, or Azure-specific services (Cosmos DB, Functions, AKS) for coursework or personal projects and want to learn enterprise cloud without bill anxiety. The no-credit-card requirement means zero risk of surprise charges.

entries.name: MATLAB Campus-Wide / Online
prose: Full toolbox suite + browser MATLAB if your uni licenses it.

**vs** Python (NumPy/SciPy) / GNU Octave: Python is free forever and more employable in industry, but won't run Simulink models or satisfy professors who grade `.m` files. Octave is syntax-compatible for basics but lacks toolboxes. Use MATLAB when the curriculum demands it; learn Python in parallel for career portability.
entries.pick: your coursework requires Simulink, Signal Processing, or Control Systems toolboxes that cost thousands commercially — the campus license bundles them all at zero cost. Also essential if professors hand out `.m` homework files with no alternative accepted.

entries.name: Notion Education
prose: Plus-class notes; Pack adds extra AI responses.

**vs** Obsidian / Logseq (free, local-first): Obsidian is free forever with no vendor lock-in and works offline, but lacks real-time collaboration and requires plugin setup for databases/kanban. Notion wins if you collaborate on group projects or prefer structured databases; Obsidian wins if you want ownership of your `.md` files post-graduation.
entries.pick: you organize everything — notes, project boards, reading lists, job applications — in one tool and want the Plus plan's unlimited blocks, file uploads, and AI features without paying $10/mo. School email verification is instant.

entries.name: Perplexity Pro Student
prose: Research AI with citations — often 1 year free.

**vs** ChatGPT Plus / Google Scholar: ChatGPT hallucinates citations; Perplexity's inline sources let you verify instantly. Google Scholar is authoritative but requires you to read and synthesize manually. Perplexity sits between them — AI speed with citation accountability.
entries.pick: you write research papers or need to quickly synthesize sources with proper citations — Perplexity Pro gives you unlimited Pro searches with source links, making it a turbo-charged literature review tool that actually shows where claims come from.

entries.name: Unity Student
prose: Unity Pro Editor for verified students 16+.

**vs** Godot / Unreal Engine: Godot is fully free and open-source but has a smaller asset ecosystem and weaker console export. Unreal is free until $1M revenue but demands beefy hardware and C++ comfort. Unity Student hits the sweet spot for 2D/mobile/VR prototyping on modest hardware with the largest tutorial ecosystem.
entries.pick: you're building games or interactive 3D experiences and want the Pro runtime features (dark theme aside — splash screen removal, runtime profiling, and priority bug fixes) without the $2k/yr price tag. Essential for game dev courses and portfolio pieces.

entries.name: Termius Premium (Pack)
prose: SSH synced across laptop and phone.

**vs** native SSH + config file / Blink (iOS): A plain `~/.ssh/config` is free and works great on one machine, but doesn't sync to mobile or handle SFTP visually. Blink is iOS-only and pricey post-student. Termius wins on cross-platform sync and team snippet sharing while the Pack license lasts.
entries.pick: you SSH into servers from multiple devices (laptop, phone, tablet) and want your hosts, keys, and snippets synced everywhere with a polished UI — especially useful when managing cloud VMs, lab machines, or homelab boxes from anywhere.

entries.name: LocalStack (Pack)
prose: Full AWS emulator — practice without burning credits.

**vs** AWS Free Tier / real AWS sandbox: Real AWS teaches you billing and IAM reality but punishes mistakes with charges. LocalStack lets you `terraform apply` fearlessly and run integration tests offline. Use LocalStack for fast dev loops; validate on real AWS only before deploy.
entries.pick: you're learning AWS (Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, SQS, API Gateway) and want to iterate locally without worrying about credits or accidentally leaving resources running. The Pro license adds persistence, IAM enforcement, and advanced services that the free Community edition lacks.

KeePass is offline-only and clunky on mobile. 1Password wins on developer UX — but export your vault before the year ends and decide if the paid price is worth it post-student.
entries.pick: you juggle dozens of accounts (school, GitHub, cloud consoles, APIs) and want a password manager that also handles SSH keys, CLI secrets, and `.env` injection via Developer Tools — solving both security hygiene and dev workflow in one app.

entries.name: Figma Starter
prose: Anyone can design with free Starter limits.
entries.pick: you're not a student (or can't be bothered with yearly verification) and just need a real vector/UI tool for side projects. Three files is plenty for a portfolio site, a mobile mockup, and a playground.

alternatives.name: Figma Education:
alternatives.text: Education gives you unlimited files and team libraries, but locks usage to non-commercial. Starter lets you ship commercial work — just with fewer files open at once.

entries.name: Autodesk Education
prose: AutoCAD, Fusion 360, Maya, Revit — renewable yearly.
entries.pick: your coursework requires parametric CAD (mechanical parts in Fusion 360), architectural BIM (Revit), or film-grade 3D animation (Maya). These are industry-standard desktop apps with no browser equivalent.

alternatives.name: Blender:
alternatives.text: Blender covers organic modeling and animation for free, but lacks parametric CAD constraints and BIM workflows. If your professor specifies Revit drawings or STEP exports, Autodesk is the only free path.

entries.name: Adobe Creative Cloud Student
prose: All Apps cheaper — still a subscription.
entries.pick: your workflow demands Photoshop, Premiere, or After Effects specifically — because your team shares .psd/.aep files, or an internship requires Adobe deliverables. The discount makes the ~$23/mo sting less, but it still stings.

alternatives.name: Figma + DaVinci Resolve:
alternatives.text: For UI design + video editing alone, Figma (free) plus DaVinci Resolve (free) covers 80% of use cases at $0. Adobe only wins when you need the exact Adobe file format or a tool like Illustrator's print-press output.

entries.name: Godot
prose: Open-source game engine. No student ID needed.
entries.pick: you want to build a 2D or 3D game and own every line of your engine. GDScript is beginner-friendly, the editor runs on potato hardware, and you can ship commercially on Steam/itch.io with zero royalties or fees.

alternatives.name: Unity/Unreal:
alternatives.text: Unity charges a runtime fee past $200K revenue; Unreal takes 5% after $1M. Godot takes nothing, ever. Trade-off: fewer AAA-ready rendering features and a smaller asset marketplace — fine for indie and jam-scale games.

entries.name: Canva Education

fields.Limits: While verified edu · not a commercial design seat

prose: Canva Pro features free for verified students and teachers.
entries.pick: you need quick social media graphics, slide decks, or print posters without learning Figma or Illustrator. The drag-and-drop template library is unmatched for non-designers who still want polished output.

alternatives.name: Figma Education:
alternatives.text: Figma is a precision UI/UX tool for developers and designers building interfaces. Canva is a marketing/content tool for fast visual assets. If you're designing app screens, use Figma; if you're making an event flyer in 10 minutes, use Canva.

entries.name: DigitalOcean (Pack)
prose: Platform credit for droplets and App Platform.
entries.pick: you want real Linux VMs (droplets) you fully control — SSH in, install anything, run Docker — or a simple App Platform deploy with zero Kubernetes overhead. Best bang-per-credit for hosting side projects that need a static IP and root access.

alternatives.name: Heroku (Pack):
alternatives.text: Heroku gives you push-to-deploy simplicity but zero SSH and no raw VM. DigitalOcean gives you the whole machine. Pick DO when you need custom Nginx configs, background workers, or GPU experimentation; pick Heroku when you just want `git push` and done.

entries.name: Heroku (Pack)
prose: Simple PaaS credit for 24 months.
entries.pick: you want the fastest path from `git push` to a live URL — no Dockerfiles, no infrastructure YAML, no SSH. The 24-month runway means your capstone demo stays online through graduation without babysitting.

alternatives.name: DigitalOcean (Pack):
alternatives.text: DO gives you a whole VM to configure yourself. Heroku abstracts all of that away: add a Postgres add-on with one click, scale dynos with a slider. You trade control for speed — ideal when shipping matters more than learning ops.

entries.name: MongoDB Atlas Credits (Pack)
prose: Stacks on top of free M0 forever tier.
entries.pick: your app speaks MongoDB (Mongoose, Motor, or the native driver) and you want a managed cluster with backups, search indexes, and Charts without paying until $50 runs out. The free University cert is a résumé line that actually signals competence.

alternatives.name: Supabase/PlanetScale free tiers:
alternatives.text: Those are relational (Postgres/MySQL). Atlas wins if your data is document-shaped (nested JSON, variable schemas). If you need joins and strict types, use a relational free tier instead.

entries.name: AWS Educate
prose: Learning paths, badges, sandboxed labs.
entries.pick: you want to learn AWS services (Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, EC2) hands-on in sandboxed labs without risking a surprise bill. The badges look good on LinkedIn and the labs teach real console workflows — but you can't deploy your own production app here.

alternatives.name: DigitalOcean/Heroku credits:
alternatives.text: Those give you real hosting for real projects. AWS Educate is a classroom — you learn the AWS way, but you don't get a public URL you can put in a portfolio. Use Educate for learning, DO/Heroku for shipping.

entries.name: Namecheap .me (Pack)
prose: Free domain year for a portfolio.
entries.pick: you want `yourname.me` pointing at your portfolio site today — zero cost for 12 months with SSL included. A custom domain makes Vercel/Netlify/GitHub Pages deploys look professional instead of living on a `.vercel.app` subdomain.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Registrar:
alternatives.text: Cloudflare sells domains at cost with free DNS/proxy, but doesn't offer a free year. Namecheap's Pack deal gives you the first year free — grab it now, then transfer to Cloudflare at renewal if you want cheaper long-term pricing and built-in CDN.

categories.description: Niche gems worth knowing.

entries.name: MotherDuck
prose: DuckDB in the cloud — analytics without a warehouse.
entries.pick: you have ~1–10 GB of CSVs/Parquet and want SQL analytics without provisioning Postgres, BigQuery, or Snowflake. Local DuckDB + cloud sync means you develop on your laptop and share dashboards without infra.

alternatives.name: Supabase (for analytics):
alternatives.text: MotherDuck is columnar and designed for analytical queries on flat files; Supabase/Postgres is row-oriented and better for CRUD apps. Don't use Postgres for 5GB event aggregations.

alternatives.name: BigQuery free tier:
alternatives.text: BigQuery gives 1TB/mo query but has cold-start latency and requires GCP. MotherDuck is instant, local-first, and the free 10GB is actual storage not just query volume.

entries.name: Val Town
prose: Serverless JS as shareable vals — cron + HTTP.
entries.pick: you need a quick API endpoint, cron job, or webhook handler and don't want to set up a repo, deploy pipeline, or hosting. Each "val" is a self-contained function with a URL — perfect for glue code, bots, and prototypes.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Workers:
alternatives.text: Workers are production-grade with KV/D1/R2 bindings; Val Town is for quick-and-dirty scripts you write in a browser tab. Use Workers for real apps, Val Town for "I need this webhook in 2 minutes."

alternatives.name: GitHub Actions (scheduled):
alternatives.text: Val Town runs on its own infra with HTTP endpoints; Actions require a repo and are slower to iterate on for simple cron tasks.

entries.name: LiveKit Cloud
prose: WebRTC SFU for voice/video without Coturn ops.
entries.pick: you're building a real-time voice/video feature (classroom, telehealth, multiplayer voice chat) and refuse to run your own TURN/STUN/SFU infrastructure. Free tier gives enough minutes to prototype and demo.

alternatives.name: Daily.co:
alternatives.text: LiveKit is open-source and self-hostable if you outgrow free tier; Daily is proprietary SaaS only. LiveKit also has better AI/agent integration for voice bots.

alternatives.name: Jitsi (self-hosted):
alternatives.text: Jitsi is a full video app you deploy; LiveKit is an SDK — you build your own UI. LiveKit for custom UX, Jitsi for "I just need a meeting room."

entries.name: Tinybird
prose: ClickHouse-backed APIs from event streams.
entries.pick: you need sub-second analytics APIs over streaming event data (page views, IoT, logs) and want ClickHouse power without managing ClickHouse. Ingest → SQL pipe → published REST endpoint in minutes.

alternatives.name: MotherDuck:
alternatives.text: Tinybird is for real-time streaming ingestion + API publishing; MotherDuck is for batch analytics on files you already have. Tinybird for live dashboards, MotherDuck for ad-hoc exploration.

alternatives.name: Supabase + pg_cron:
alternatives.text: Tinybird handles millions of events/day with columnar compression; Postgres will choke on that volume. Use Supabase for your app DB, Tinybird for your analytics API.

entries.name: Svix
prose: Outbound webhook delivery (Hookdeck's dual for sending).
entries.pick: your SaaS needs to send webhooks to customers and you don't want to build retry logic, signature verification, delivery dashboards, and failure alerting from scratch. 50k msgs/mo free handles most early-stage products.

alternatives.name: rolling your own queue + retry:
alternatives.text: Svix handles exponential backoff, signing, delivery logs, and customer-facing retry UI. Building that yourself is 2–4 weeks of work you'll regret maintaining.

alternatives.name: Hookdeck:
alternatives.text: Hookdeck is for *receiving* webhooks (inbound); Svix is for *sending* them (outbound). They're complements, not competitors.

entries.name: Dub.co
prose: Link shortener with analytics — no Bitly tax.
entries.pick: you share links publicly (newsletters, social, docs) and want click analytics + custom domains without Bitly's $35/mo paywall. The free tier is generous enough for indie projects and personal branding.

alternatives.name: Bitly:
alternatives.text: Dub.co is open-source, cheaper at scale, and developer-friendly (API-first). Bitly charges for custom domains and advanced analytics that Dub includes free.

alternatives.name: just using your own redirect:
alternatives.text: Dub gives you analytics, QR codes, link previews, and expiration without writing any code. A bare Nginx redirect gives you nothing.

entries.name: Hugging Face Spaces
prose: Prototype ML demos on free CPU Spaces.
entries.pick: you want to deploy a Gradio/Streamlit ML demo that anyone can try via a URL — no server setup, no Docker, no cloud billing. Perfect for thesis demos, portfolio projects, and "try my model" links on your resume.

alternatives.name: Google Colab:
alternatives.text: Spaces gives you a persistent public URL others can visit; Colab requires the notebook to be running and shared. Spaces for demos, Colab for experimentation.

alternatives.name: Replicate:
alternatives.text: Replicate is pay-per-prediction for production inference; HF Spaces is free for CPU demos. Use Spaces to prototype, Replicate when you need GPU scale.

entries.name: Cron-job.org
prose: External cron — ping sleeping Render apps before demos.
entries.pick: your free-tier Render/Railway app sleeps after 15 minutes of inactivity and you need it awake for demos, interviews, or monitoring. Set a 14-minute ping and your app never cold-starts in front of someone important.

alternatives.name: UptimeRobot:
alternatives.text: UptimeRobot monitors and alerts when things are *down*; cron-job.org proactively *prevents* sleep by pinging on a schedule. UptimeRobot for observability, cron-job.org for keep-alive.

alternatives.name: GitHub Actions scheduled workflow:
alternatives.text: Cron-job.org has 1-minute granularity and doesn't burn Actions minutes. It's also simpler — paste a URL, set an interval, done.

entries.name: Zyte Scrapy Cloud (Pack)
prose: One Scrapy Cloud unit forever via Pack.
entries.pick: you have Scrapy spiders and want them running on a schedule in the cloud without maintaining a server or Docker cron. The Pack gives you one persistent unit — enough for a personal data pipeline that scrapes daily.

alternatives.name: self-hosted Scrapy + cron:
alternatives.text: Zyte handles scheduling, log storage (120 days), and scaling without you babysitting a VPS. The tradeoff is vendor lock-in to their platform.

alternatives.name: Apify free tier:
alternatives.text: Apify is broader (Puppeteer, Playwright, any scraper); Zyte is Scrapy-native. If your spiders are already Scrapy, Zyte deploys them as-is with zero rewrite.

alternatives.text: More integrations and wider data history, but requires signup and has stricter free limits.

entries.name: WeatherAPI
prose: Weather data with current conditions, forecasts, historical data, and astronomy (sunrise/sunset). The free tier is generous at 1M calls/month but limited to 3-day forecasts.
entries.pick: you need high volume on free tier and 3-day forecast is enough, or you want astronomy data included.

alternatives.name: Open-Meteo
alternatives.text: Higher free volume ceiling but requires a key; Open-Meteo is simpler for quick prototypes.

catalogs.label: LLM & AI
catalogs.description: Free LLM inference, embeddings, local models, and AI developer tooling — models, limits, and compatibility.

categories.label: Embeddings
categories.description: Text and multimodal embedding APIs for RAG, search, and similarity

entries.name: Voyage AI
prose: Top-tier embedding quality, especially for code (voyage-code-3) and retrieval tasks. Benchmarks consistently near the top on MTEB. Free credits on signup let you prototype RAG pipelines.
entries.pick: you need the highest-quality embeddings for retrieval/RAG and can afford PAYG after free credits.

alternatives.name: Together Embeddings
alternatives.text: Better quality for code and retrieval; Together is cheaper at scale with open-weight models.

entries.name: Together Embeddings
prose: Open-weight embedding models hosted. Because the models are open (BGE, E5), you can self-host later without vendor lock-in. OpenAI SDK compatible.
entries.pick: you want OpenAI-compatible embeddings from open-weight models with an escape hatch to self-host.

alternatives.name: Voyage AI
alternatives.text: Lower quality ceiling but open models mean you can self-host; Voyage is proprietary but higher quality.

entries.name: Cloudflare Workers AI (Embeddings)
prose: Embedding generation at the Cloudflare edge. Pairs naturally with Vectorize (their vector DB) and Workers for end-to-end RAG without leaving the Cloudflare ecosystem.
entries.pick: your RAG stack is on Cloudflare (Workers + Vectorize + AI) and you want zero-hop embeddings.

alternatives.name: Voyage AI
alternatives.text: Lower quality models (BGE vs Voyage) but free and integrated into Cloudflare; Voyage is better quality but separate infra.

categories.label: Inference
categories.description: Cloud LLM inference providers with free tiers for chat, completion, and tool use

entries.name: OpenRouter
prose: Meta-router across 200+ models from dozens of providers. Free-tagged models run at $0 with rate limits. Pay-per-token for everything else. One API key works across all providers, making it ideal as a failover entry point.
entries.pick: you want one API key to access many providers and use `:free` models for development/side projects.

alternatives.name: Groq
alternatives.text: OpenRouter is a router (many providers); Groq is a single ultra-fast inference provider. OpenRouter's free models rotate; Groq's free tier is more predictable.

entries.name: Groq

fields.Free Tier: generous daily token limits (varies by model)

prose: Fastest inference available — LPU hardware delivers tokens at 500+ tok/sec for Llama 70B. Free tier has daily token/request caps but is extremely fast. Ideal for real-time chat and tool-calling loops.
entries.pick: you need the fastest token generation and your use case fits within daily free limits.

alternatives.name: Cerebras
alternatives.text: Both are speed-focused. Groq has more model variety; Cerebras is similarly fast but with fewer models.

entries.name: Cerebras
prose: Wafer-scale inference hardware. Similar speed story to Groq with extremely fast generation. Currently offers fewer models but competitive on Llama variants.
entries.pick: you want an alternative fast provider to Groq for failover, or Groq's daily limits are exhausted.

alternatives.name: Groq
alternatives.text: Similar speed; Groq has more model options. Good as a failover provider in a multi-provider router.

entries.name: Google AI Studio
prose: Google's AI models via API. Gemini Flash is fast and cheap (generous free tier). Supports multimodal (images, audio, video), function calling, and structured output. The OpenAI-compatible endpoint means you can use the OpenAI SDK.
entries.pick: you need multimodal (image/video understanding), long context (1M tokens), or the most generous free daily quota.

alternatives.name: Groq
alternatives.text: Gemini is multimodal and has longer context; Groq is faster for text-only chat. Gemini free tier is more generous per day.

entries.name: Mistral
prose: European AI lab's API. Mistral Nemo (12B) is free-tier eligible and good for structured output and function calling. Mistral models tend to be efficient for their size class.
entries.pick: you want a strong small model (Nemo 12B) with good instruction following and structured output.

alternatives.name: Google AI Studio
alternatives.text: Smaller models, more predictable outputs for structured tasks; Gemini is more capable but heavier.

entries.name: Cloudflare Workers AI
prose: Run inference at the edge alongside your Cloudflare Workers. No cold starts for AI if your app is already on Workers. 10k neurons/day free, then usage-based. Good for adding AI features to existing Workers apps.
entries.pick: your app is already on Cloudflare Workers and you want AI inference with zero extra infra.

alternatives.name: Groq
alternatives.text: Slower inference but integrated into Cloudflare edge; no separate billing. Groq is faster but requires separate API management.

categories.label: Local
categories.description: Run LLMs locally on your own hardware — zero API cost, zero rate limits

entries.name: Ollama

fields.Models: Llama 3.3, Qwen 2.5, Mistral, Phi-4, DeepSeek, Gemma 3, CodeLlama, etc.

prose: The simplest way to run LLMs locally. One binary, `ollama pull llama3.3` and you're inferencing. Manages model downloads, quantization selection, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. Works on macOS (Metal), Linux (CUDA/CPU), Windows.
entries.pick: you want the easiest path to local LLMs with zero configuration and OpenAI SDK compatibility.

alternatives.name: LM Studio
alternatives.text: Ollama is CLI-first and scriptable; LM Studio is GUI-first with a nice chat interface. Both expose the same OpenAI-compatible server.

entries.name: LM Studio

fields.Models: any GGUF model from HuggingFace (browse + download in-app)

prose: Desktop GUI for running local LLMs. Browse/download models from HuggingFace, adjust parameters visually, and run an OpenAI-compatible local server. Nice for experimentation and non-CLI users.
entries.pick: you prefer a GUI for model management and want to easily compare different models in a chat interface.

alternatives.name: Ollama
alternatives.text: Better UX for exploration and comparing models; Ollama is better for scripting, automation, and server deployments.

entries.name: llama.cpp
prose: The foundational C++ inference engine that Ollama and LM Studio are built on. Direct control over quantization, context length, batch size, GPU layers. Maximum performance tuning at the cost of more manual setup.
entries.pick: you need maximum control over inference parameters, custom builds, or are embedding inference into a larger system.

alternatives.name: Ollama
alternatives.text: llama.cpp is the engine; Ollama wraps it with model management and ease-of-use. Use llama.cpp directly for custom builds or performance tuning.

categories.label: Observability
categories.description: LLM cost tracking, tracing, evaluation, and monitoring tools

entries.name: Langfuse

fields.Free Tier: generous free cloud tier, self-host unlimited

prose: Open-source LLM observability: traces, cost tracking, latency, prompt management, evaluations, and datasets. Integrates with LangChain, OpenAI SDK, Vercel AI SDK, and more. Self-host for free or use their cloud.
entries.pick: you want full LLM observability (traces + costs + evals) and the option to self-host.

alternatives.name: Helicone
alternatives.text: Langfuse is deeper (evals, datasets, prompt versioning); Helicone is simpler (proxy + dashboard).

entries.name: Helicone
prose: One-line integration: swap your OpenAI base URL to Helicone's proxy and get cost tracking, caching, rate limiting, and request logs. Zero code change beyond the base URL.
entries.pick: you want the simplest possible LLM cost/usage visibility — change one URL and get a dashboard.

alternatives.name: Langfuse
alternatives.text: Simpler setup (just a proxy URL) but less depth; Langfuse has evals, datasets, and self-hosting.

categories.label: Tooling
categories.description: Developer tools, SDKs, and frameworks for building AI applications

entries.name: Vercel AI SDK

fields.Models: any provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, Ollama, etc.)

prose: TypeScript SDK for building AI-powered UIs with streaming, tool calling, and structured output. Provider-agnostic: one interface for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, Ollama, and more. React/Next.js hooks for streaming chat UI.
entries.pick: you're building AI features in a Next.js/React app and want streaming UI with provider switching.

alternatives.name: Continue.dev
alternatives.text: Different tools. AI SDK is for building AI into your app; Continue.dev is an AI assistant in your IDE.

entries.name: Continue.dev

fields.Models: Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint

prose: Open-source AI code assistant for VS Code and JetBrains. Point it at Ollama for $0 code completion and chat, or use any API provider. Tab autocomplete, inline editing, chat with codebase context.
entries.pick: you want a free GitHub Copilot alternative that works with local models or cheap API providers.

alternatives.name: Vercel AI SDK
alternatives.text: Continue.dev is an IDE tool for your workflow; AI SDK is a library for building AI features into apps.

entries.name: Mem0
prose: Managed memory layer for AI agents. Stores user context, preferences, and conversation history so agents remember across sessions. Self-hostable or use their cloud.
entries.pick: you're building agents that need to remember user context across sessions without reinventing memory storage.

alternatives.name: Langfuse
alternatives.text: Different layer. Mem0 is memory (what to remember); Langfuse is observability (what happened).
